To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Indian, African and Middle Eastern rock phosphate sources are not suitable for direct application for rice cultivation in India.
the rock phosphates of India were found to be inferior to those of USA and other countries in terms of their reactivity and agronomical effectiveness for direct application for rice.
The Indian rock phosphatic materials were less reactive and less efficient for rice production in the three soil orders, when applied to moist soils, prior to flooding and planting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the comparative study of reactivity of Indian, US (Idaho, Missouri and Tennessee), African and Middle East (Egyptian) rock phosphates.

the evaluation of the agronomic effectiveness of various rock phosphates for direct application in flooded rice soils, and to correlate their reactivity in the field and in the laboratory with their chemical composition, especially the degree of CO3, F, and NH4 -cit substitution for PO4.
the development of a simple method of estimating the relative reactivity of francolite rocks for direct application for rice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Indian rock phosphates were less reactive than North Carolina rock phosphate and hence their use in direct application for growing paddy on laterite, alluvial and red soils is not recommended.
the Indian rock phosphates are poor in P, low in reactivity and hence less effective in rice growing, when applied to moist soils, 15days prior to flooding and planting rice.
the rock phosphates from the USA, Africa and the Middle East were more reactive, more efficient and hence better than the Indian rock phosphates for the growing of rice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the North Carolina rock phosphate is more reactive than the other sources, because of its higher degree of CO3/ PO4 and F/P2O, mole ratio substitution, higher apatite content and higher citrate extractable soluble P in eight successive citrate extractions.

the Indian, US, Middle East and African rock phosphates are not as reactive for direct application for rice, when applied to moist soils 15 days prior flooding and transplanting, as the North Carolina rock phosphate, which is known to be very effective for rice production.
the North Carolina rock phosphate, with its higher citrate soluble P, was more reactive in the soils and hence more efficient in promoting growth and P uptake by the crop.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Indian rock phosphates were not as effective as superphosphate, in respect of rice grain yield and P uptake by the plant, when applied directly to soil, in the pot experiment.
the Indian rock phosphates were less reactive than North Carolina rock phosphate, and hence were less effective for growing rice on the lateritic, red and black soils.
the Indian rock phosphates, which have been used for the direct application to rice for over two decades, have been found to be less effective than North Carolina rock phosphate.
